events.excerpt: Proposal Type: Protocol Upgrade Hi, I’m Andrea Federici, Senior Solutions Engineer at OP Labs. I prepared this proposal in collaboration with Matthew Cruz from the OP Labs team. Neither OP Labs nor I, nor any other entity mentioned, represent or speak on behalf of the Optimism Foundation. Executive Summary Upgrade 21 is an L1 smart contract upgrade for OP Stack chains, shipped in op-contracts/v9.0.0 . It has no hardfork and no activation timestamp: every change is applied through a signed superchain-ops execution on L1. It contains the following changes: ETHLockbox as custody and pause identifier — every chain gets an ETHLockbox that cannot be disabled, and it becomes the only identifier for a chain-specific pause. Chains whose ETH is still in the OptimismPortal have it moved into the lockbox in the upgrade transaction. Chains that already use a lockbox are unchanged. Custom gas token chains get a lockbox but keep custody in the portal. Permissionless deleteProvenWithdrawal — anyone can delete a withdrawal proof whose dispute game resolved in favor of the challenger or was blacklisted. Proofs on valid games are unaffected. OPCM v9.0.0 and StandardValidator — removes the startingAnchorRoot upgrade override, lowers batched-upgrade gas, and adds validator checks for the new lockbox

events.excerpt: Release Notes Node version 11.2.0 is a pre-release version of cardano-node that is not yet recommended for use on mainnet. Its headline change is the move to the new cardano-config library for reading node configuration: the node now understands a versioned configuration "envelope" alongside the existing flat format, and the configuration files published for each network are now in the envelope format. It also extends the gRPC interface, continues the groundwork for the Dijkstra era, Leios and Peras, and fixes several operator-facing bugs. Highlights: New configuration format. Configurations are read through cardano-config . Existing flat configurations still work. The new envelope format ( $schema / Version / MinNodeVersion / Configuration ) is schema-validated. New cardano-node config migrate , cardano-node config schema and cardano-node config resolve subcommands convert, describe and check a configuration. The shipped network configs are now enveloped and cannot be read by nodes older than 11.2 . gRPC over HTTP/2. The gRPC server can now listen on a TCP address/port, in plaintext (h2c) or with TLS ( --grpc-listen-address / --grpc-listen-port , --grpc-tls-* ), instead of only a unix socket. New gRPC methods ReadMempool , WatchMempool and ReadEraSummary , plus server reflection

Abstract Deploying and distributing private smart contracts, confidential L2/Validium state diffs, or permissioned intent payloads across Ethereum’s public P2P and Data Availability (DA) layers currently faces a fundamental metadata bottleneck. Even when contract bytecode or state is symmetrically encrypted, existing Broadcast Encryption (BE) and Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) schemes require attaching an explicit cleartext header specifying either the authorized recipient indices, covering subsets, or the target access tree. In this post, we propose an architectural framework based on Stealth Attribute-Based Broadcast Encryption (Stealth ABBE) over BLS12-381 ( Zenodo Preprint ) for zero-metadata delivery of private contracts and encrypted state on Ethereum. By reformulating broadcast access control as a homomorphic blind Reed–Solomon decoding problem over 𝔽 256 using carry-free Base-3 packing in exponential ElGamal ciphertexts (𝔾 1 × 𝔾 1 ), Stealth ABBE achieves: O(1) Broadcast KEM Size (24.1 KiB amortized): Fits comfortably inside a single EIP-4844 blob (~19% of one 128 KiB blob) regardless of the total participant count N . Zero Visible Headers or Revocation Lists (0 Bytes): Access policies, cohort rosters, and revocation states are algebraically absorbed into the non-system
events.headline: Stealth ABBE over BLS12-381: Zero-Metadata Broadcast of Private Contracts & Encrypted State via EIP-4844 Blobs

events.excerpt: Executive summary Ethereum’s upcoming enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS) introduces new ways for validators to participate in block-building markets. Most importantly, it enables builders to compete directly for block proposals, with payments guaranteed by the Ethereum protocol, reducing the need for trusted intermediaries. This proposal seeks to preserve the principles of Lido’s existing MEV Policy while adapting it to ePBS: maximizing rewards for stakers, supporting open and competitive block-building markets, and ensuring that Node Operators (NOs) do not favor particular builders or withhold MEV rewards. Following the discussion in Lido’s call for an updated MEV policy . It proposes a two-track approach: 1. An open, permissionless market where Lido validators can accept bids from any builder meeting Ethereum’s protocol requirements, provided payments are guaranteed by the protocol. 2. A vetted market where builders and intermediaries offering additional payments outside Ethereum’s guarantees must be approved through Lido’s Allowed List. Both tracks apply regardless of how a bid arrives: via p2p, a direct connection, or through one of the available sidecars. APR is maximized as operators can source from the full market; MEV hiding remains detectable because every bid

events.excerpt: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. See how agents access your site Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. events.excerpt: Status: a design proposal for discussion. Nothing in this post is decided. Changes described here would need to go through governance with token holders’ approval. Dates are aims, not commitments. 1. Context Two complementary developments were proposed that could affect validators in the near future. The first is the move to Metanodes, described in a forum post by Adrian . Besides relay chain consensus, validators would take on node roles that the ecosystem currently funds separately, starting with collation and full nodes for Asset Hub and People Chain, potentially with further roles such as Bulletin Chain as opt-in. Over time, this could replace the separately funded RPC, collator and bootnode setups. For validators, it would mean more work per node and stronger hardware. The hardware requirements are published in the Polkadot docs. The second is a smaller active set. A forum post by Jan-Jan proposes reducing it step by step via three referenda, one week apart (600 → 500 → 400 → 320), with the aim of completing the reduction before the end of 2026. The first referendum has already been submitted. Each step would require Fellowship whitelisting and a token holder vote. Together, these developments call for recalibrating validator rewards. events.excerpt: Hello, I’ve opened a PR for a new opcode, SLOTDURATION . It pushes the duration of the current slot, in milliseconds, onto the stack. PR: Add EIP: SLOTDURATION Opcode by Amxx · Pull Request #12619 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub Open questions: Current duration or historical lookup? The draft returns the current duration. The Rationale describes an alternative where the opcode takes a slot number and returns the duration in effect at that slot, or 0 for future slots. That would let contracts like Lido’s compute correct timestamps across duration changes. The cost is that the execution layer would have to keep the duration schedule. Which is more useful? Milliseconds. I chose ms to match SLOT_DURATION_MS and to support L2s with 100–250 ms block times. Any objections? 0 for “no regular interval.” Is this the right sentinel for on-demand chains, and should L1 execution clients still reject 0 ? Execution-layer decoupling. EIP-8198 deliberately keeps the execution layer unaware of the slot duration. The draft keeps the EL config-free, but it does add a header field. Is that acceptable to the EIP-8198 authors and to client teams? 3 posts - 3 participants Read full topic
events.headline: EIP-8484: SLOTDURATION Opcode

events.excerpt: CometBFT v0.38.25 can’t read an ML-DSA public key. Its PubKeyFromProto knows Ed25519 and secp256k1, and its MaxSignatureSize is 64 bytes, while an ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309. That’s the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs, and the v29.1.0 release candidate from Monday keeps it. The Quarterly says post-quantum consensus keys shipped with SDK v0.55 and CometBFT v0.40, and that the Hub moves to v30 once ibc-go carries v0.55. Before any chain lets its validators use those keys, I wanted to know what breaks on the other side of its IBC connections, so I read the rotation code and the light clients. The SDK docs already say every counterparty must upgrade before the first validator rotates. This is what I’d add to that. v0.38.26 is enough for a Go counterparty The docs ask counterparties for CometBFT v0.40. On the 0.38 line there’s a smaller step. v0.38.26 (13 August, PR 6028 ) backports only ML-DSA decoding and verification, “for the purposes of verification of IBC connections with counterparty chains that are on v0.40”, and raises MaxSignatureSize to 3,309. It doesn’t let the chain itself use the key. So a chain on SDK v0.53 doesn’t need the v0.55 migration for its own clients of an ML-DSA chain, a patch release on the line it’s on covers it. What a counterparty runs is in its /cosmos/base/t

With the value built into the binary, the network can shorten its unbonding time without every operator editing config.toml . ⚠️ Check Before You Update seid now ignores trust-period in the [statesync] section of config.toml . State sync uses a trust period of 112 hours on pacific-1 , atlantic-2 and arctic-1 . If config.toml sets trust-period to another value, seid start logs a warning that begins with statesync.trust-period is set in config.toml each time the node starts. Earlier seid versions wrote trust-period = "168h0m0s" into config.toml , so most nodes will log this warning. To stop it, remove the trust-period line. The node runs normally with or without the line ( #4690 ). If you use state sync, use a recent trust height. The block at trust-height must be less than 112 hours old. events.excerpt: For some, rules pose limitations. For others, like Microsoft Research Manager Mike Walker, they’re opportunities. Walker’s fascination with rules and their role in the social order has allowed him to find success professionally and personally, from uncovering weaknesses in networked systems to redefining how computers are trained to fend off cyberattacks to pushing the limits of a reliable mode of transportation—the bicycle—in ultra-endurance racing. In this conversation with Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu, Walker describes how his participation in hacker culture led him to a career building next-generation cyber defense, including his work developing the first all-machine hacking tournament. Along the way, he reflects on why effective security depends on understanding trust and context, what competitive hacking taught him about teamwork and collective intelligence, and how an early lesson reshaped his understanding of leadership. He also tackles an important question: are today’s networked systems any safer than they were a decade ago? events.excerpt: Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking. For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences. AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast. Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials. Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time. AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours. And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. events.excerpt: Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it. I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet. Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors. Two weeks and a slow prototype Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school. That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow. events.excerpt: You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished. AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure. To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire : a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next. How it works Zero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section. events.excerpt: In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind , I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system. Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany: Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change. In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm. We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves. Still in its early stages, but definitely something th

Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin , NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own. events.excerpt: The regression test the Fellowship added for the dotUSD incident fits on one screen. Alice holds 1,000 dotUSD and no DOT. She sends one WithdrawAsset for her dotUSD plus 1 DOT. dotUSD sorts first and gets withdrawn, the DOT withdrawal fails, the instruction errors. Before the fix, her balance came back and the supply didn’t. Parity’s incident review went up yesterday ( review ) and explains it at a high level. I wanted to see both halves in code, the supply that drifted and the pool that priced it, so I read the fix in polkadot-sdk and that test ( tests.rs at 7b27d43 ). All of it is fixed and public, and I’m only looking at the code here, not at the disclosure timeline. The credit that dropped too late Since polkadot-sdk PR #10384 (merged 16 February 2026) the XCM executor keeps real imbalances in holding instead of plain numbers. That PR was actually written to keep total issuance correct during XCM programs. WithdrawAsset takes each asset from the origin as a Credit and collects them in a local called withdrawn . withdrawn was declared before TransactionalProcessor::process(|| ...) and only moved into holding in an .and_then after it. events.excerpt: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines. A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co. , a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “ XCPE ” (named after one of the malware’s core code components). The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group. The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location.
